newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran's Rafsanjani not decided on Saudi haj visit.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Rafsanjani not decided on Saudi haj visit.

text.p: Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani has not yet decided whether to accept a Saudi invitation to perform haj, the pilgrimage to Moslem holy sites in the kingdom, in April, Iran's haj supervisor said.
The official Iranian news agency IRNA said late on Sunday that Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri made his comments in the holy city of Medina in Saudi Arabia where he arrived on Sunday.
He said Rafsanjani had received the invitation from Saudi Crown Prince Abdullah when the two held rare talks in Islamabad earlier in March on the sidelines of an Islamic summit.
Rafsanjani "has not yet taken any decision in this regard", Reyshahri said.
A Saudi newspaper on Friday quoted Iran's ambassador to Riyadh as saying Rafsanjani was expected to make his first official visit to Saudi Arabia in April to perform haj.
Rafsanjani last travelled to Saudi Arabia at the start of the 1979 Iranian revolution on a personal visit to perform haj.
Reyshahri said a visit by Rafsanjani would "strengthen bilateral relations and will bring the governments of the Islamic republic of Iran and Saudi Arabia closer".

Iran's ties with Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil producer and custodian to Islam's two holiest shrines, have been tense since Iran's Islamic revolution and are usually further strained in the run-up to haj every year.

Iran insists on holding political rallies in Mecca mainly to denounce the United States and Israel in defiance of Saudi bans on political activity during haj. Riyadh says haj is a religious duty and should not be politicised.
In 1987 Saudi police clashed with demonstrators in an Iranian-led rally in Mecca killing about 400 people, mainly Iranians. Iran boycotted the haj for the next three years.

Iranian leaders have called on pilgrims to stage a rally at this year's haj, despite repeated Saudi warnings in the past two months against any political activity during the pilgrimage. Haj, which this years falls in the middle of April, attarcts two million Moslems every year.

Tehran has been trying to improve its ties with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf Arab states and analysts say its desrie for better relations has been reflected by a softer tone used by the media and officials towards Saudi Arabia in the past few weeks even when calling for the rallies.
Iran's Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati has said his visit to Saudi in March as part of a Gulf tour opened up a new chapter in relations between Tehran and Riyadh.
